panels.rationale: Single-panel H&E micrograph of a human breast resection specimen; caption and in-text mentions explicitly establish invasive ductal carcinoma with infiltrating cords/tubules and desmoplastic fibrosis, matching the configured disease and histology findings. Lymphovascular invasion finding is recorded as explicitly absent in the text, so it is not a positive manifestation. [raw subtype: invasive ductal carcinoma, no special type (NST)]
panels.attribution_text: Sato et al. Arterial Calcification Disappearance in Breast Imaging: A Key Indicator for Transition to Invasive Ductal Carcinoma.. Diagnostics (Basel, Switzerland) 2024. doi:10.3390/diagnostics14070727. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 5.
panels.figure_caption: The hematoxylin- and eosin-stained specimen shows cancer cells with mildly enlarged, oval nuclei forming small cords and tubular structures, infiltrating and proliferating with fibrosis. Ultimately, a diagnosis of invasive ductal carcinoma was established (invasion diameter, 11 mm; estrogen receptor, J-Score 3b; progesterone receptor, J-Score 3b; human epidermal growth factor receptor 2, score 2; fluorescence in situ hybridization, negative; Ki-67, 7.5%).
in_text_mentions: Pathological examination results confirmed that the breast mass was an invasive ductal carcinoma (Figure 5). Surgical pathology also indicated thick blood vessels within the tumor, suggesting a correlation with the initially observed calcified artery. However, there were no clear signs of tumor invasion into the blood vessels. Notably, although the patient had calcifications (atherosclerosis) in the arteries of her normal breast tissue, calcifications were not observed within or around the tumor-associated arteries (Figure 6).

in_text_mentions: The IBC NST is historically classified into different grades (G) with varying prognostic and predictive values. Prognostically, G1 is the best, while G3 is the worst. panels.figure_caption: Grayscale ultrasound images of a 65‐year‐old woman with a right breast mass. (A) Shows a hypoechoic mass with parallel orientation, irregular shape, microlobulated margins, posterior acoustic shadowing, and a surrounding echogenic halo. (B) Illustrates a suspicious hypoechoic ipsilateral axillary lymph node without an echogenic hilum Histopathological and immunohistochemical analysis confirmed a grade 3 invasive ductal carcinoma (IDC) that is ER positive, PR negative, HER2 negative, with a Ki‐67 index of 15%. The axillary lymph node was involved by IDC.
in_text_mentions: Figures 1, 2, 3 illustrate ultrasound findings in three patients with breast masses, showcasing various sonographic features such as hypoechoic lesions, irregular shapes, non‐parallel orientation, spiculated or indistinct margins, posterior acoustic shadowing, and echogenic halos. These sonographic patterns were frequently observed in cases with specific histopathological and molecular features, as illustrated in Figures 1, 2, 3. This highlights the diagnostic utility of ultrasound imaging in evaluating breast lesions.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Mammography panel from a patient with IDC, showing an irregular ill-circumscribed isodense breast mass with microlobulated margin, consistent with the article's IDC focus. B: Second mammographic view from the same IDC case, showing the same irregular ill-circumscribed isodense mass with microlobulated margin. C: Gray-scale ultrasound of the IDC patient showing an irregular, ill-circumscribed heterogeneous hypoechoic breast mass, matching the IDC ultrasound description. D: Hematoxylin and eosin histopathology from the IDC patient showing infiltrating nests of pleomorphic cells with desmoplastic stroma, consistent with invasive ductal carcinoma.

in_text_mentions: nical, US, and MG imaging features. Significant differences in age, menopausal status, family history, microcalcification morphology, and vascularity grade were observed between the breast adenosis and IDC groups in the training cohort (p<0.05). No significant difference was found between the two groups in glandular type, architectural distortion, mass, asymmetric focal density, shape, orientation, posterior feature, margin, calcification, and echo pattern (p>0.05). The GSUS features, MG features and histopathological characteristics of breast lesions or IDC are summarized in Figures 4 and 5 .

panels.rationale: Single grayscale breast ultrasound of a 57-year-old woman's left breast mass; caption states histopathology and immunohistochemistry confirmed grade 1 invasive ductal carcinoma (ER+/PR+/HER2-, Ki-67 6%). The panel shows the classic sonographic manifestation of IDC: an irregular, spiculated hypoechoic mass with posterior acoustic shadowing, matching the provided finding key. No skin is visible, so skin tone is null; age group adult per caption.
panels.attribution_text: Moradi et al. Sonographic Correlations With Histological Grade and Biomarker Profiles in Breast Invasive Ductal Carcinoma.. Cancer reports (Hoboken, N.J.) 2025. doi:10.1002/cnr2.70288. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Grayscale ultrasound image of a 57‐year‐old woman with a left breast mass. The lesion exhibits a hypoechoic echo pattern, non‐parallel orientation, irregular shape, spiculated margins, posterior acoustic shadowing, and a surrounding echogenic halo. Histopathological and immunohistochemical analysis confirmed a grade 1 invasive ductal carcinoma (IDC) that is ER positive, PR positive, HER2 negative, with a Ki‐67 index of 6%.
in_text_mentions: Figures 1, 2, 3 illustrate ultrasound findings in three patients with breast masses, showcasing various sonographic features such as hypoechoic lesions, irregular shapes, non‐parallel orientation, spiculated or indistinct margins, posterior acoustic shadowing, and echogenic halos. These sonographic patterns were frequently observed in cases with specific histopathological and molecular features, as illustrated in Figures 1, 2, 3. This highlights the diagnostic utility of ultrasound imaging in evaluating breast lesions.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: H&E-stained histology of a real patient breast tumor showing invasive glandular carcinoma with desmoplastic stroma; caption and article title attribute it to low-grade invasive ductal carcinoma (NOS). [raw subtype: low-grade infiltrating duct carcinoma (NOS) with tubular features] B: Immunohistochemical (cytokeratin cocktail CK7/18) stain of the same patient's invasive carcinoma, with the caption explicitly confirming the presence of invasive ductal carcinoma; the finding is an IHC staining pattern not represented in the supplied vocabulary. [raw subtype: low-grade infiltrating duct carcinoma (NOS) with tubular features] C: Immunohistochemical myoepithelial marker stain (P63/CK5/14) of a real patient's invasive ductal carcinoma demonstrating absence of myoepithelial cells around invasive glands, a finding not covered by the supplied vocabulary. [raw subtype: low-grade infiltrating duct carcinoma (NOS) with tubular features] D: Second...
panels.attribution_text: Al-Refai et al. Immunohistochemical Staining Characteristics of Low-Grade Invasive Ductal Carcinoma Using the ADH5 Cocktail (CK5/14, P63, and CK7/18): A Potential Interpretative Pitfall.. Diagnostics (Basel, Switzerland) 2023. doi:10.3390/diagnostics13182966. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: ADH5 stain showing the expected pattern of staining. An invasive carcinoma showing a glandular growth pattern and a low nuclear grade with desmoplastic stroma (H&E) ((A), ×20). The cytokeratin cocktail stain confirms the presence of invasive ductal carcinoma (CK7/18 red); inset for the positive internal control ((B), ×20). The absence of corresponding myoepithelial stains (loss of brown P63 and CK5/14) confirms the invasive carcinoma; inset for the positive internal control ((C,D), ×20).
in_text_mentions: Four of the 44 cases analyzed (9.1%) showed an expected staining pattern for ADH5. Specifically, two cases were identified as tubular carcinomas, and the other two cases were classified as low-grade infiltrating duct carcinoma (NOS) cases with tubular features. In the expected staining patterns, brown staining (representing P63 and CK5/14) was lost around the invasive glands, accompanied by diffuse red staining (representing CK7/18). This staining pattern was consistent with the expected results Figure 1.

plate_findings.evidence: round mass with subtle irregular margins ... peripheral enhancement with a small central hypovascular area

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Sagittal DCE-MRI in a 38-year-old woman with biopsy-proven grade III invasive ductal carcinoma; panel shows an enhancing breast mass with irregular margins and central hypovascularity, consistent with the captioned malignancy. B: Axial delayed-phase DCE-MRI of the same invasive ductal carcinoma, showing the enhancing mass with central hypointensity; included as part of the same patient imaging. C: Diffusion-weighted image (b=700 s/mm2) of the known invasive ductal carcinoma, captioned as a hyperintense mass with a central hypointense component; no exact vocabulary finding key applies. D: ADC map from the same patient with invasive ductal carcinoma, showing a manually traced ROI and reported ADC value; included as a patient-specific diagnostic image, though no exact vocabulary finding key applies.
panels.attribution_text: Moutinho-Guilherme et al. Correlation between apparent diffusion coefficient values in breast magnetic resonance imaging and prognostic factors of breast invasive ductal carcinoma.. Porto biomedical journal 2019. doi:10.1016/j.pbj.0000000000000027. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Thirty-eight-year-old woman with invasive ductal carcinoma in the upper external quadrant of the left breast. A, Sagittal dynamic contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging 2 minutes after contrast enhancement identified a round mass with subtle irregular margins. The lesion was characterized by peripheral enhancement with a small central hypovascular area. B, Axial dynamic contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging 10 minutes after contrast enhancement (delayed phase). C, On diffusion-weighted images acquired with a b value of 700 s/mm2, the tumor appeared as a hyperintense mass with a central hypointense component. D, A region of interest (ROI) within the margins of the lesion was manually traced on apparent diffusion coefficient maps, avoiding the central part. Apparent diffusion coefficient value was equal to 1.01 × 10–3 mm2/s. At histopathology, the lesion was defined as a grade III invasive ductal carcinoma. At the immunohistochemical analysis, hormonal receptor status was positive (estrogen and progesterone receptors), Ki67 expression was 60% and human epidermal growth factor receptor type 2 (HER2) status was equal to 0 (negative). Axillary lymph node status was negative.
in_text_mentions: The ROI was manually drawn in the slice in which the cancer presented a greater diameter (Fig. 1). Apparent necrotic or cystic components were avoided by referring to other MRIs. In cases with multifocal or multicentric masses the largest tumor was selected. The image analysis was performed by 2 radiologists with 2 and 20 years of experience on breast MRI. The final ADC value for each patient was obtained by consensus between the 2 radiologists, with the lowest being the preferred number.

[raw subtype: no special type (NOS)] C: H&E histology of invasive breast carcinoma, NOS, showing a stromal area with abundant tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (>50% sTILs) and scattered pleomorphic tumor cells, corresponding to the captioned scoring category. panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (a, b). a: Mediolateral oblique mammogram of the right breast in a 57-year-old woman showing a cluster of pleomorphic microcalcifications (arrow), which was surgically proven invasive ductal carcinoma; caption and article title directly attribute the finding to IDC. b: Recombined/contrast-enhanced mammographic image of the same patient showing an irregular mass with unpurified ground-glass and solid enhancement (arrow); surgically proven IDC, so the panel is a patient image of the target disease, though the enhancement texture pattern is a less common descriptor (variant).
panels.attribution_text: Cheung et al. Contrast-Enhanced Mammographic Features of In Situ and Invasive Ductal Carcinoma Manifesting Microcalcifications Only: Help to Predict Underestimation?. Cancers 2021. doi:10.3390/cancers13174371. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: Mass with unpurified ground glass enhancement: In a 57-year-old woman, the biopsied microcalcifications were a group of pleomorphous microcalcifications (arrow) in the lower region of the right breast on LM in MLO view (a). REI revealed an associated irregular mass with ground glass and solid enhancement (arrow) (b). Finally, it was surgically proven to be IDC.
in_text_mentions: gy was classified as nonmass (clump appearance without a bulging outline) or mass (shaped appearance with a bulging outline). The textures of enhancement consisted of pure ground glass (transparent to underlying) (Figure 1) and unpurified ground glass (with a nontransparent solid part) (Figure 2). For the reason of unmeasurable enhancement intensity on REI, we used the terms of ‘ground glass’ and ‘solid’ appearances to distinguish the texture of ‘weaker’ and ‘stronger’ enhancement relevant to the transparency to the underlying even though they were infrequently used as enhancement descriptors.

in_text_mentions: specimen was sent for histopathological examination. During the processing of a specimen, a careful examination of the excised breast tissue revealed a 1.2 cm mass within a dilated duct, suspicious of intraductal carcinoma. The mass was located in close proximity to an area of prominent lymphocytic infiltration. The surrounding breast tissue showed evidence of chronic inflammation and fibrosis. Microscopic examination of that suspicious mass confirmed the presence of IDC. The tumor was characterized by atypical ductal epithelial cells with high nuclear grade and comedo necrosis (Figures 2, 3).

in_text_mentions: In the second biopsy from the axilla, the specimen consisted of similar pleomorphic cells as seen in the original breast biopsy, arranged in nests, cords, sheets, and trabeculae in an extremely necrotic background (Fig. 2). Immunohistochemical stains were performed, and the anaplastic cells were immunoreactive for AE1/AE3 and CK7, with a higher Ki-67 proliferative index and a focal area of Synaptophysin positivity. However, the tumor cells were negative for GATA3, mammaglobin, ER, PR, HER2, CK20, chromogranin, and CD56.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: H&E histology of a human metastatic lymph node from primary breast cancer, showing infiltrating tumor cells consistent with invasive ductal carcinoma. B: H&E histology of a human cervical biopsy showing metastatic invasive ductal carcinoma with infiltrating cords and small nests; cervical metastasis is an uncommon site. C: H&E histology of a human hysterectomy specimen showing metastatic invasive ductal carcinoma with cords, small nests, and occasional tubules.

Asia Oceania journal of nuclear medicine & biology 2020. doi:10.22038/aojnmb.2019.41658.1284. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 3.
panels.figure_caption: F-18 FDG whole body maximum intensity projection image and selected transaxial CT, PET and PET/CT fusion images of the breasts of a 58 year-old patient with right invasive ductal carcinoma who underwent right mastectomy and axillary dissection. Histopathology showed primary tumor in lower inner quadrant, 2.4×1.7×1.5 cm in size, with retroareolar extension and multiple microscopic foci (primary tumor grade 3, pathological stage T2N2A) as well as ductal carcinoma insitu surrounding the main tumor. PET showed the hypermetabolic primary tumor (SUVmax=12) (arrow) and multiple smaller hypermetabolic foci surrounding the primary tumor and also in retroareolar region (SUVmax=3.4, 3.7, 4.1 and 4.4) (short arrows) as well as right axillary lymph node metastases (SUVmax=8.9). Diffuse uptake is also seen in the skin of the right breast, indicating extension of the tumor
in_text_mentions: PET, surgery was mastectomy and multifocal uptake was around the primary tumor in 3, and around and away from primary tumor in 1 patient (Figure 2). In 2 of 11 patients with multifocal tumor on pathology, PET showed unifocal uptake (primary tumor), no other foci. In one of these patients, size of the multifocal tumor was 4 mm which is below PET resolution. In a patient with microscopic multifocal tumor and mastectomy as surgical procedure, PET showed multiple foci of uptake (at least 5 foci with highest SUVmax of 4.4) adjacent, around and away from the primary tumor (SUVmax of 12) (Figure 3).

panels.attribution_text: Oshita and Oura. Invasive Ductal Carcinoma of the Breast With an Uncommon Widespread Thick Hyperechoic Pattern: A Case Report.. Cureus 2026. doi:10.7759/cureus.103491. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 4.
panels.figure_caption: Pathological findings A) The tumor had solid areas (asterisk) and widespread cancer cells in the fat tissue (arrows), using the fibrous tissue as a stalk (open circle). B) Magnified view showed atypical cells densely growing, with microvoids (arrows) around cancer cell clusters. C) Magnified view showed cancer cell infiltration into the fat tissue (arrows). D) Immunostaining showed estrogen receptor positivity (Allred score 7). E) Immunostaining showed progesterone receptor negativity. F) Immunostaining showed human epidermal growth factor receptor type 2 equivocality. G) Immunostaining showed a Ki-67 labeling index of 35%. H) D2-40 immunostaining showed cancer cell involvement in the lymphatic vessels (arrows). I) Two normal-sized lymph nodes (arrow) had cancer cell metastasis (asterisks).
in_text_mentions: ectomy and axillary dissection, with written informed consent about the operative option from the patient. Postoperative pathological study showed cancer cells growing in solid and trabecular fashions, spreading in 25-mm sizes, with microvoids around cancer cell clusters, marked fat invasion, and two metastatic lymph nodes. Immunostaining of the tumor showed estrogen receptor positivity (Allred score 7), progesterone receptor negativity, human epidermal growth factor receptor type 2 equivocality (fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) negative), and a Ki-67 labeling index of 35% (Figure 4).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Ultrasound of the breast in a case report of invasive ductal carcinoma, showing the uncommon widespread thick hyperechoic pattern described in the article title; the asterisk-marked hypoechoic areas are also present. B: Axillary ultrasound from the same invasive ductal carcinoma case report, showing an abnormal lymph node with a diffuse punctate hyperechoic pattern; the node is not enlarged but is part of the axillary staging in this cancer patient.

panels.figure_caption: Ultrasound findings Ultrasound showed widespread, thick hyperechoic areas with indistinct margins (arrows), hypoechoic areas (asterisk) (A), and a lymph node with a diffuse punctate hyperechoic pattern (arrow) in the axilla (B).
in_text_mentions: Ultrasound showed widespread, thick hyperechoic areas, 31 mm in size, with indistinct margins and adjacent hypoechoic areas. The hypoechoic areas had irregular shapes, focal internal punctate high echoes, and internal vascularity. Ultrasound further showed no axillary lymph node swelling, but one lymph node, which had a diffuse punctate hyperechoic pattern (Figure 2).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Craniocaudal mammographic view of the patient's biopsy-confirmed invasive ductal carcinoma of the right breast, showing an irregular iso-dense mass with obscured margins, matching the mammographic IDC finding vocabulary. B: Mediolateral oblique mammographic view of the same IDC-confirmed mass, showing the irregular iso-dense lesion described in the caption. C: Color Doppler ultrasound of the biopsy-proven invasive ductal carcinoma showing an irregular hypoechoic solid mass with indistinct margins and increased vascularity; the axillary lymphadenopathy finding is not applicable since the caption/in-text state no suspicious lymphadenopathy, so it is omitted. D: Maximum-intensity-projection dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI of the IDC-confirmed breast mass showing an enhancing irregular lesion with the adjacent vessel sign and prominent ipsilateral breast vascularity as stated in the caption.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: H-E stained section of the breast primary showing infiltrating solid nests/cords of pleomorphic tumor cells, explicitly captioned as invasive ductal carcinoma; article title and in-text (ER/PR/HER-2 negative, ypT3N3) confirm the target disease. Classic histologic appearance of IDC-NST. B: Endoscopic view of the ~1 cm elevated fundic lesion (white arrow) that proved to be a gastric metastasis of the patient's breast invasive ductal carcinoma; the article title explicitly attributes this gastric lesion to IDC of the breast, so the panel shows a disease manifestation (metastatic spread) rather than a separate primary gastric cancer. No IDC-specific endoscopic finding exists in the vocabulary, hence proposed finding; typicality variant as gastric metastasis is an uncommon site. C: H-E section of the endoscopic gastric biopsy showing a poorly differentiated, non-glandular carcinoma. In context (case report of gastric metastasis from breast...

in_text_mentions: The second biopsy reported high-grade invasive ductal carcinoma, no special type, with a nesting pattern and lympho-vascular invasion (Figure 5). Immunohistochemistry showed estrogen receptor (ER) and progesterone receptor (PR) positive, human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2)/neu 3+ (positive), and a Ki-67 index of 40%. A clinical diagnosis of inflammatory carcinoma of the left breast was made although pathognomonic histological findings like dermal lymphatic tumour emboli were not reported.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (a, b, c). a: H&E section shows cohesive nests of pleomorphic malignant epithelial cells infiltrating stroma, consistent with the caption's 'malign epithelial tumor cells'; the article title and text establish these as metastatic invasive ductal carcinoma of the breast (uterine metastasis). b: Immunohistochemistry showing strong GCDFP-15 positivity in the same pleomorphic tumor cell population, a marker supporting breast (invasive ductal carcinoma) origin of the metastasis, as stated in the text. c: Low-power pancytokeratin immunostain demonstrating extensive epithelial (cytokeratin-positive) tumor infiltration of the myometrium/endometrium, confirming the metastatic invasive ductal carcinoma as described in the text.

panels.figure_caption: Pathological examination. Pathological microscopic examination demonstrating malign epithelial tumor cells ((a); hematoxylin-eosin, ×100), immunohistochemical staining positive for GCDFP-15 ((b); ×200), and pancytokeratin ((c); ×40).
in_text_mentions: tion revealed lesions that caused diffuse thickening of the uterus wall (Figure 1). Endometrial sampling was performed for confirmation of the diagnosis. She underwent total abdominal hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy. Breast carcinoma metastases in endometrium and myometrium were confirmed histopathologically and immunohistochemically with positivity of pancytokeratin and gross cystic disease fluid protein-15 (GCDFP-15) and negativity of Melan A, CD 10, caldesmon, and alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) (Figure 2). She is under the exemestane treatment that was commenced after the surgery.

B: Fundus photograph of the right eye in an IDC patient showing subretinal yellow nodular bulges, the clinical manifestation of ocular metastasis from IDC; no matching vocabulary finding key. C: Fundus angiography of the same IDC patient's right eye demonstrating leakage and hypofluorescence within the metastatic lesion; supports ocular IDC metastasis but has no matching vocabulary finding. D: H&E (X200) of the right ocular tumor in a confirmed IDC patient showing infiltrating cords and nests of pleomorphic cells with hyperchromatic nuclei, the histologic hallmark of invasive ductal carcinoma. panels.figure_caption: Imaging and pathological data of OM in IDC patients. (A) Ultrasound examination of ocular (right eye). Hypoechoic mass with an irregular shape could be seen in the posterior pole of the right eye. Echo attenuated behind the mass and infiltration could be seen around the mass. (B) Fundus photography (right eye). Under the retina, yellow nodular flat bulges with unclear boundaries could be seen. (C) Fundus angiography (right eye). Fluorescence leakage and low fluorescence in the lesion could be seen. Blood vessels were visualized in the field of vision. (D) Hematoxylin‐eosin staining of the right ocular tumor, X200. Infiltration of cancer cells arranged in cords and nests with hyperchromatic nuclei could be seen in the tissue. Cellular atypia was obvious.
in_text_mentions: the medical records systems. The inclusion criteria were as follows: (i) Patients were diagnosed with primary breast cancer at The First Affiliated Hospital of Nanchang University. (ii) Ophthalmic examinations in OM patients indicated intraocular space‐occupying lesions. (iii) The pathological diagnosis of IDC was confirmed by the Pathology Department of The First Affiliated Hospital of Nanchang University. In addition, patients with metastatic breast cancer or primary ocular malignant tumor were excluded from the study. Imaging data and pathological results of patients are shown in Figure 1.

panels.attribution_text: Abdallah et al. Enhancing histopathological image classification of invasive ductal carcinoma using hybrid harmonization techniques.. Scientific reports 2023. doi:10.1038/s41598-023-46239-0. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 5.
panels.figure_caption: On the left, we present examples of central patches, which constitute the majority within the entire histopathological slide. On the right, we showcase examples of border patches. These two distinct types of patches are invariably present in histopathological studies, as they result from the segmentation of a whole slide.
in_text_mentions: Figure 5 illustrates examples of patches from a histopathological slide following unsupervised clustering. One cluster comprises images of border regions, while the other encapsulates images of central regions, thereby underscoring the need for intra-slide harmonization to mitigate such variabilities. Additionally, this intra-slide variability is manifest not only between different cluster patches but also within the same cluster patches across various classes, as illustrated in Fig. 6.

Upon identifying the most efficient outlier detection algorithm, we applied it to the entire dataset. The dataset was then divided into two subsets: one containing atypical patches (border patches) and another consisting of non-atypical patches (primarily central patches from the histopathological slides). The results of this classification are presented in Fig. 5.

panels.figure_caption: H&E stain slide shows histopathological features of IDC.
in_text_mentions: An ultrasound of the left axilla revealed a mass measuring 12.6 × 8.4 × 4.5 cm, located near the anterior border of the latissimus dorsi muscle and inferior to the axillary vein. The mass exhibited heterogeneous echotexture and irregular margins, suggestive of malignancy. Additionally, three enlarged ALNs with irregular borders were identified. A core needle biopsy of the mass, guided by ultrasound, confirmed the presence of IDC (Fig. 2). Furthermore, an ultrasound-guided biopsy of the suspicious ALNs confirmed malignancy.

Ultrasound-guided core biopsy of this node was performed, and histopathologic evaluation confirmed metastatic ductal carcinoma, establishing nodal involvement consistent with N1 disease. panels.figure_caption: Positive AE1/AE3 immunohistochemical staining of the invasive ductal carcinoma component (arrows). The malignant melanoma is immediately adjacent (arrowheads) with no staining.
in_text_mentions: tologically unique neoplasms immediately adjacent to one another (Figure 1). The first is IDC with focal squamous differentiation. Juxtaposed with this was a distinct malignant population of metastatic melanoma. The IDC was graded as provisional Nottingham grade III. The malignant melanoma component stained positive for SOX10 and Pan-melanoma markers (Figure 2) and was negative for AE1/AE3. The IDC tumor cells were positive for AE1/AE3 (Figure 3) and GATA3, but negative for estrogen receptor, progesterone receptor, and Her2 (1+). The patient was referred to a clinical oncologist for treatment.

panels.stage: metastatic to colon; 6 of 11 lymph nodes positive
panels.rationale: Patient immunohistochemistry image from a case of metastatic invasive ductal carcinoma involving the colon. The caption and in-text mention identify the tumor cells as CDX-2 negative, supporting the diagnosis of metastatic breast carcinoma; arrows annotate tumor cells. The panel shows tumor histology/immunophenotype rather than a primary breast lesion, so typicality is variant.
panels.attribution_text: Katz et al. Colonic Obstruction from an Unusual Cause: A Rare Case of Metastatic Invasive Ductal Carcinoma to the Colon.. Cureus 2018. doi:10.7759/cureus.2588. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 6.
panels.figure_caption: Immunohistochemistry fo CDX2 Tumor cells are negative with CDX-2 (arrows). Colonic crypt cells are positive (top of image).
in_text_mentions: The tumor was transmural with involvement of serosal fat through the lamina propria and percolated between the colonic crypts with six out of 11 lymph nodes positive. Immunohistochemical staining was positive for cytokeratin 7, estrogen receptor (Figure 3), and GATA-3 (Figure 4), and negative for cytokeratin 20 (Figure 5), caudal-related homeobox transcription factor - 2 (CDX-2) (Figure 6), MELAN-A, CD 56, and synaptophysin. This was consistent with metastatic breast cancer. Further stains were positive for E-cadherin (Figure 7), consistent with her history of invasive ductal carcinoma.

panels.rationale: Single grayscale transabdominal/pelvic ultrasound of a human patient showing the uterine mass described in the caption and in-text (4.8x3.2 cm lesion thickening the uterine wall). The article title and text attribute the uterine lesion to metastasis of invasive ductal carcinoma, so the panel depicts a specific, though unusual (atypical) manifestation of the target disease. The lesion is a heterogeneous hypoechoic mass with posterior attenuation; the only matching vocabulary term is the hypoechoic-mass-with-shadowing entry, applied here with visual evidence. No age or ethnicity data given; no skin visible. [raw subtype: metastatic invasive ductal carcinoma (uterine metastasis)]

in_text_mentions: The current diagnostic tests and gynecologic examination revealed a 4.8x3.2 cm lesion that caused diffuse thickening of the uterine wall (Figure 1). She was referred to the gynecologic oncology department for further evaluation. An endometrial biopsy was performed to eliminate any endometrial pathology caused by tamoxifen treatment, which was found negative.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (a, b, c, d). a: Serial mammogram panel showing a small nodular density in the right breast that was later proven to be invasive ductal carcinoma; initially mimicking an intramammary lymph node. b: Follow-up mammogram showing minor interval change in the nodular density that was subsequently confirmed as invasive ductal carcinoma. c: Serial mammogram showing increasing density and partially obscured margins in the nodular lesion proven to be invasive ductal carcinoma. d: Final mammogram showing a larger, denser lesion with indistinct margins, consistent with invasive ductal carcinoma.

panels.rationale: Single immunohistochemistry panel from a patient with metastatic invasive ductal carcinoma to the colon, showing membranous E-cadherin positivity indicated by arrows. It is a real patient histology image supporting the target disease; no skin, ethnicity, or age information is provided.
panels.attribution_text: Katz et al. Colonic Obstruction from an Unusual Cause: A Rare Case of Metastatic Invasive Ductal Carcinoma to the Colon.. Cureus 2018. doi:10.7759/cureus.2588. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 7.
panels.figure_caption: Immunohistochemistry stain for E-cadherin Positive membranous stain for E-cadherin (arrows).
in_text_mentions: The tumor was transmural with involvement of serosal fat through the lamina propria and percolated between the colonic crypts with six out of 11 lymph nodes positive. Immunohistochemical staining was positive for cytokeratin 7, estrogen receptor (Figure 3), and GATA-3 (Figure 4), and negative for cytokeratin 20 (Figure 5), caudal-related homeobox transcription factor - 2 (CDX-2) (Figure 6), MELAN-A, CD 56, and synaptophysin. This was consistent with metastatic breast cancer. Further stains were positive for E-cadherin (Figure 7), consistent with her history of invasive ductal carcinoma.
